prompt:
Technical note on staged weight transfers in a mixed-device inference server.

A mixture-of-experts transformer keeps most expert weight matrices in system memory and streams only the experts a router selects. Each prompt batch touches many experts, and every touched expert must be resident on the compute device before its matmul runs. The transfer path therefore sits directly on the critical path of prompt processing.

A straightforward implementation issues a host-to-device copy straight from the file-backed mapping. The source pages are pageable. The driver cannot DMA from pageable memory without extra bookkeeping, so each call spends a long time inside the submission call itself before any bytes move. When thousands of small-to-medium copies are issued per prompt, the submission overhead dominates the wall clock even though the theoretical link bandwidth is modest.

A staging ring improves this situation. The server allocates a small number of pinned host slots once, at context initialization. A copy is split into chunks no larger than one slot. The host copies the chunk bytes into a free pinned slot with a plain memcpy, then submits an asynchronous device copy from that slot and records an event on the compute stream. The next chunk can be filled while the previous chunk is still transferring, because a different slot is free. The slot returns to the free pool when its event completes.

The ring is bounded. Its memory is fixed at allocation time and never grows. If the allocation fails, the feature disables itself permanently for the lifetime of the context and every subsequent copy takes the original path. The ring is opt-in through an environment variable and only activates for multi-row expert copies; single-token decoding keeps using the ordinary path. A chunk of sixteen mebibytes fits the largest observed expert range, and the trailing alignment padding of the weights buffer is copied as part of the byte range, byte for byte.

Correctness is verified without a model. The staged destination bytes must equal the bytes produced by the original path for sparse expert ids, consecutive ids, the first expert at offset zero, the last expert at the end of the buffer, ranges that cross the chunk boundary, and the padding tail. Sentinel bytes outside the copied range must be untouched. Reuse of the two slots must pass through at least three cycles. Allocation failure must fall back cleanly and log once.

The performance question is narrow. If the submission stall is the bottleneck, overlapping the host fill with the in-flight transfer should reduce prompt latency by a measurable amount while leaving single-token generation untouched or slightly better, because the decode path is unchanged. Decode speed is therefore a regression gate, not a target: it must not fall by more than two percent. Prompt latency for secondary requests must not degrade by more than three percent.

Robustness matters as much as speed. A long prompt produces many batches and therefore many thousands of staged calls; the slot state machine must survive all of them. Repeated requests in one session must reuse prefix caches normally. Speculative decoding must keep accepting and rejecting draft tokens exactly as before; a rejected draft must roll the context back to a checkpoint without disturbing the ring. Cancelling a streaming request must restore the prompt state from a checkpoint and leave the next ordinary request correct. Graceful shutdown must drain outstanding slot events, free pinned memory, and leave no orphan processes or CUDA errors.

Memory accounting closes the list. The pinned budget is thirty-two mebibytes of host slots plus less than one mebibyte of metadata. Swap usage must stay exactly zero. Device-side staging remains zero; the destination of every chunk is the original weights buffer at its original offset.

Appendix one: expected transfer shape. Expert ranges are uneven. The median range is close to one mebibyte, the ninetieth percentile is a little below three mebibytes, the ninety-ninth percentile is above five mebibytes, and the largest observed range is near fifteen mebibytes. Every range fits inside a single slot, so a range maps to one or two chunks and never more than two. Two slots are enough to keep the host busy while a transfer is in flight; a third slot was explicitly not implemented because the two-slot schedule already hides most of the fill.

Appendix two: counters. The backend logs one activation line when the ring is created and one summary line at shutdown that reports the number of staged calls and the number of chunks. The counters are cumulative for the process lifetime. A prompt-only request and the same prompt with generation must produce the same counters, because generation must not touch the ring at all. A mismatch between those two totals means decode has started to use the bulk path by accident, and the run is invalid.

Appendix three: session expectations. Short prompts contain well under a hundred tokens and stress generation rather than transfer. Long prompts contain more than five hundred and twelve tokens so that the scheduler emits several batches and the ring cycles through its slots repeatedly. Prefix caching must remain enabled inside the session: a repeated identical prompt must be served from cache with a tiny prompt-evaluation time. Streaming cancellation must leave the slot idle and clean; the following request must produce the same bytes it produced before the cancellation.

Appendix four: stop conditions. Any CUDA error, any out-of-memory condition, any nonzero swap delta, any hang, any output that differs between arms beyond deterministic expectation, or any prompt degradation beyond the stated gate stops the block immediately and invalidates nothing that was already recorded.

End of note.

Question: according to this note, which specific part of inference does the staging ring accelerate, and which metric serves as the regression gate?
